MUQATIL:2:263/r1.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:263/r1.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:263/r1.claim: A kind reply and forgiveness toward a poor person who asks but receives nothing are better than charity followed by injury or reproach.

MUQATIL:2:263/r2.author: Muqātil b. Sulaymān
MUQATIL:2:263/r2.speaker: author
MUQATIL:2:263/r2.claim: God has no need of people's charity and is forbearing, delaying punishment for those who reproach and hurt its recipient.

TAB-FULL:v4p658/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p658/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p658/r1.claim: A kind word or prayer for a Muslim brother, together with excusing and concealing his difficult circumstances, is better than charity followed by injury.

TAB-FULL:v4p658/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p658/r2.speaker: الضحاك
TAB-FULL:v4p658/r2.claim: Al-Dahhak says it is better to keep one’s wealth than give it and then reproach or harm the recipient.

TAB-FULL:v4p658/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p658/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v4p658/r3.claim: God is independent of people’s alms and forbearing, delaying punishment for those who remind recipients and hurt them.

TAB-FULL:v4p658/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v4p658/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
TAB-FULL:v4p658/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses the Rich as complete in wealth and the Forbearing as complete in forbearance.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r1.speaker: النبي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r1.claim: A report reaching Amr ibn Dinar says the Prophet declared that no charity is dearer to God than a kind word, citing this verse.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r2.speaker: قتادة
IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r2.claim: Qatada says God knew some people would remind others of gifts, disliked it, and therefore commended kind speech and forgiveness over charity followed by harm.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r3.speaker: السدي
IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r3.claim: Al-Suddi explains “God is self-sufficient” as meaning that God has no need of your charities.

IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r4.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNABIHATIM:v2p516#2/r4.claim: Ibn Abbas says God informed His servants of His forbearance, compassion, generosity, vast mercy, and forgiveness.

NAHHAS:v1p333/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v1p333/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v1p333/r2.claim: قول معروف may have an omitted predicate; مغفرة is a subject and خير its predicate, meaning a forgiving act beats hurtful charity.

THALABI:v2p259/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p259/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p259/r10.claim: A kind, gracious answer to a petitioner is “known good”; al-Kalbī defines it as a sincere prayer for one's brother in his absence, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk as speech reconciling people.

THALABI:v2p259/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p259/r11.speaker: محمد بن جرير
THALABI:v2p259/r11.claim: Muḥammad ibn Jarīr explains forgiveness as the donor's overlooking the poor person's need-related conduct; al-Kalbī and al-Ḍaḥḥāk also call it pardon for an insult.

THALABI:v2p259/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p259/r12.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p259/r12.claim: Because a poor person may be distressed by refusal and answer harshly or complain, the giver is urged to pardon him; this is better than a gift followed by harm.

THALABI:v2p259/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p259/r13.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p259/r13.claim: Harm after charity includes reproaching the petitioner for asking, complaining about him, finding fault, or other hurtful remarks.

THALABI:v2p260/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p260/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p260/r1.claim: God has no need of human charity; He could enrich everyone, but gave wealth to test the rich in gratitude and left the poor to be tested in patience.

THALABI:v2p260/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p260/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v2p260/r2.claim: God is forbearing because He does not hasten punishment for someone who reproaches or harms with a gift.

THALABI:v2p260/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p260/r3.speaker: عبد الرحمان السليماني
THALABI:v2p260/r3.claim: A report from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulaymānī, client of ʿUmar, attributes to the Prophet advice not to interrupt a petitioner and to answer with dignity, gentleness, a small gift, or gracious refusal.

THALABI:v2p260/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v2p260/r4.speaker: بشر بن الحرث
THALABI:v2p260/r4.claim: Bishr ibn al-Ḥārith recounts a dream in which ʿAlī said that a poor person's confidence in God is even better than a rich person's charitable kindness.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r10.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r10.claim: The Prophet warns that one who reminds others of what he gave will not be addressed, regarded, or purified by God on Judgment Day and will suffer painful punishment.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r6.claim: Good speech replaces reproach and harm: one should kindly draw near when giving or pray for the asker when refusing.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r7.claim: Forgiveness may mean pardoning the asker's offense, being kept from sin, declining to give (Ibn Bahr), or concealing the poor person's state without exposing it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r8.speaker: ابن بحر
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r8.claim: Ibn Bahr interprets forgiveness in this context as leaving the charity and withholding it.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p337/r9.claim: The harm after charity may be reminding the recipient of the gift or taunting them for poverty; good speech is better than such charity either for the recipient or with God.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r1.claim: قول معروف is kind, pleasing speech and a gracious response to a petitioner; ʿAta says it can be a kind promise, and generally it is accepted rather than rejected by people.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r2.speaker: ابن جرير
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r2.claim: He interprets مغفرة as concealing the petitioner's need.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r3.speaker: عطاء والحسن
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r3.claim: They interpret it as forgiving a petitioner who speaks rudely after being refused; pardon is better than charity followed by reproach or hurt.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r4.claim: A poor person may react sharply to refusal without a gift, so God commands pardon and teaches that this is better than giving and then hurting the petitioner.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v4p411/r5.claim: God needs no human charity; He invites people to give so He can reward them. Ghani is the opposite of need.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:261-263/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:261-263/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:261-263/r4.claim: A kind word is a gracious reply to a petitioner, and forgiveness means overlooking the petitioner if he presses after being refused.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:261-263/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:261-263/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:2:261-263/r5.claim: Kind speech and pardon are better than charity followed by reproach; God needs no human charity and patiently delays punishment for those who boast of it.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r1.claim: A kind reply to a petitioner, or a kindly promise, is 'recognized speech'; al-Kalbi says it can be a prayer for a fellow believer in their absence, and al-Dahhak links it to reconciliation.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r2.speaker: الكلبي والضحاك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r2.claim: Al-Kalbi and al-Dahhak say forgiveness means overlooking the wrongdoer; it can also mean forgiving a poor person's rude persistence when refused.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r3.claim: A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by hurtful reminders or reproach.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p326/r4.claim: God needs no one's charity and, being forbearing, does not hasten punishment of one who reminds and hurts recipients.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r1.claim: A good word means a courteous, gracious reply.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r2.claim: Forgiveness may mean excusing an irritating petitioner, God's forgiveness earned by a gentle refusal, or the petitioner's forgiving the refusal.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r3.claim: The indefinite subject can be predicated of as ‘better’ because its descriptive qualification makes it specific.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p340/r4.claim: God has no need of a giver who reminds and harms, and His forbearance delays immediate punishment; this restraint signals displeasure and threat.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r1.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r1.claim: Kind speech—prayer, reassurance, and hope in God’s reward—and pardon for a needy person’s faults are better than a gift that is outwardly charity but inwardly empty; kind speech earns reward, while harmful giving does not.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r2.speaker: المهدوي وغيره
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r2.claim: Al-Mahdawī and others supply an implied “more fitting” in the syntax: a good word is more fitting, and pardon is better.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the supplied wording because it dulls the rhetorical force; the omitted wording should be understood as present in meaning.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r4.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r4.claim: Here forgiveness means overlooking a needy person’s defect and difficult circumstances.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r5.speaker: النقاش
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r5.claim: Al-Naqqāsh says pardon can mean forgiving a petitioner who speaks harshly after being refused.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v1p357/r6.claim: God has no need of such a donor’s gift and patiently gives possible offenders time.

TABRISI:2:263#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:263#2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:263#2/r1.claim: God needs no charity or worship; he commands these acts for people's need of their reward.

TABRISI:2:263#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:263#2/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:263#2/r2.claim: God is forbearing and does not hasten punishment; in context this especially means he delays punishment for those who remind and harm recipients.

TABRISI:2:263/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:263/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:263/r1.claim: God is ghani because he owns all things and can do all things; ghina is freedom from need, while ghina can also mean song or sufficiency.

TABRISI:2:263/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:263/r2.speaker: قيس بن الحطيم
TABRISI:2:263/r2.claim: Qays ibn al-Hatim uses غنيانها for a woman's singing in his verse.

TABRISI:2:263/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:263/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:263/r3.claim: A gracious word means a kind, decent reply to a petitioner; other readings make it a good prayer, kind promise, or speech reconciling people.

TABRISI:2:263/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:263/r4.speaker: الجبائي
TABRISI:2:263/r4.claim: Al-Jubba'i interprets forgiveness as being spared sin and therefore safe from punishment; another view takes it as shielding the petitioner's request.

TABRISI:2:263/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:263/r5.speaker: الحسن
TABRISI:2:263/r5.claim: Al-Hasan says forgiveness means the person asked to give pardons the petitioner for mistreatment, such as asking at a bad time, pressing, or entering without permission.

TABRISI:2:263/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:263/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:2:263/r6.claim: Kind words and pardon surpass a gift followed by harm because the injurious giver gains neither the money's benefit nor its afterlife reward, whereas kindness and pardon earn reward.

TABRISI:2:263/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:2:263/r7.speaker: محمد
TABRISI:2:263/r7.claim: A prophetic report says to let a petitioner finish before answering with dignity and gentleness, either a modest gift or gracious refusal, since unseen observers watch how God's gifts are used.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#2/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#2/r1.claim: A kind word to a poor person might be “May God give you ease.”

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#2/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#2/r2.claim: Maghfira means concealing a fellow Muslim's need and poverty; another interpretation is forgiving a petitioner who is persistent when refused.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#2/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p318#2/r3.claim: Kind speech and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm, as explained above.

RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r1.claim: A recognized word is speech accepted by hearts and not rejected; here it means answering a petitioner kindly, while Ata glosses it as a good promise.

RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r2.speaker: عطاء
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r2.claim: Ata explains قول معروف as a good promise to the petitioner.

RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r3.claim: Maghfira may mean forgiving a poor person's harsh words when refused, since disappointment can provoke a sharp response.

RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r4.claim: Maghfira may mean receiving God's forgiveness for refusing the petitioner kindly.

RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r5.claim: Maghfira may mean concealing the needy person's circumstances and not exposing his need to someone he would rather avoid.

RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r6.claim: Another reading addresses the person asked with قول معروف and the petitioner with مغفرة: the petitioner should excuse a refusal when the requested help is unavailable.

RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r7.claim: A kind refusal is better than a gift followed by abuse because that combines benefit with harm, and the harm may outweigh the benefit; kind words bring joy without injury.

RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r8.speaker: بعض الناس
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r8.claim: Some say the verse concerns voluntary charity, because obligatory alms cannot be withheld or refused; al-Razi allows it to include obligatory charity redirected to another petitioner or poor person.

RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v7p43/r9.claim: God is independent of people's charity and commands it to reward them; He is forbearing in delaying punishment for those who taunt and harm recipients.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r1.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r1.claim: Here 'forgiveness' means concealing a needy person's deficiency and poor condition; an Arab used the phrase 'God forgive' when shame about his livelihood prevented him from giving his lineage.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r2.speaker: النقاش
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r2.claim: Al-Naqqash interprets the phrase as forgiving a persistent, rude petitioner, which is better than giving with reproach and injury.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r3.speaker: النحاس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r3.claim: Al-Nahhas says this interpretation is syntactically difficult: 'forgiveness' is the subject and 'better than charity' its predicate, with an implied act leading to forgiveness.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r4.claim: An alternative parsing makes God's forgiveness better than the particular charity donors spoil with reminders.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r5.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263#2/r5.claim: God is absolutely independent of human charity and commanded it to reward people; His forbearance means He does not punish the donor immediately for reminders and harm.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r1.speaker: النحاس
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r1.claim: Al-Nahhas parses 'kind speech' as an independent phrase with an omitted predicate; alternatively, an omitted subject makes it the commanded response.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r10.speaker: علي
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r10.claim: In the dream, Ali closes his advice with a poem about inevitable death and building for the lasting afterlife.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r2.claim: Kind speech means prayer, reassurance, and encouragement about God's reward; it is better than charity that looks charitable but earns nothing because it is followed by harm.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r3.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r3.claim: The Prophet calls a good word charity and says meeting one's brother with a cheerful face is an act of kindness; Muslim transmits the report.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r4.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r4.claim: Receive a petitioner warmly and speak gently, so that a gift earns thanks and a refusal is excused.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r5.speaker: بعض الحكماء
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r5.claim: A sage advises greeting someone in need cheerfully: if he does not thank you, at least he has an excuse for not receiving help.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r6.speaker: ابن لنكك
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r6.claim: Ibn Lankak recounts Ibn Duraid's unsuccessful appeal to a minister and quotes verses urging a patron not to resent petitioners or repel hopeful faces.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r7.speaker: رسول الله
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r7.claim: A report from Umar attributes to the Prophet an instruction to let a petitioner finish, then answer with dignity and gentleness, a small gift, or a gracious refusal; unseen beings observe how God's gifts are used.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r8.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r8.claim: The author links that report to the Muslim narration of an angel testing a leper, a bald man, and a blind man by appearing in their forms.

QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r9.speaker: بشر بن الحارث
QURTUBI-FULL:2:263/r9.claim: In a dream, Bishr asks Ali for useful advice; Ali says wealthy compassion toward the poor seeks God's reward, while poor people's dignity toward the rich rests on trust in God's promise.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:262-263/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:262-263/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:262-263/r4.claim: Qawl ma'ruf means a gracious reply; forgiveness may mean overlooking the petitioner and need, God's forgiveness for a gracious response, or the petitioner excusing the refusal.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:262-263/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:262-263/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:262-263/r5.claim: The indefinite noun can begin the sentence because it is qualified; the phrase is the predicate for both gracious speech and forgiveness.

BAYDAWI-FULL:2:262-263/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:262-263/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:2:262-263/r6.claim: God has no need of giving accompanied by reproach or harm, and He is forbearing toward those who do this rather than hastening punishment.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p129#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p129#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p129#2/r1.claim: A courteous reply and forgiveness of a petitioner, if the request burdens the person asked, are better than charity followed by hurt; alternatively, the reply earns God's forgiveness.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p129#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p129#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p129#2/r2.claim: The indefinite subject can validly take the predicate خير because it is qualified by a description.

NASAFI-FULL:v1p129#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p129#2/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p129#2/r3.claim: God has no need of a donor who reproaches or hurts the recipient; His forbearance delays punishment, which is a warning.

QASHANI:2:263-265/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:263-265/r1.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:263-265/r1.claim: Kind speech, even refusal, gladdens heart and spirit; charity benefits the body, but hurt spoils that benefit and cannot equal spiritual comfort.

QASHANI:2:263-265/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:2:263-265/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:2:263-265/r2.claim: God has no need of hurtful charity and can supply recipients from the unseen; He is patient and does not hasten punishment.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p650/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p650/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p650/r1.claim: غني is an intensive form of “need-free”; it can also mean residing, while غانية describes a woman whose beauty needs no adornment, as a cited poet says people are each self-sufficient.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r1.speaker: مفسرون غير مسمين
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r1.claim: Reported meanings of قول معروف include prayer for the petitioner, consolation and hope in God, praying privately for a fellow believer, commanding right, praise and glorification, concealing one’s own faults, politely encouraging another to give, or a good answer to a petitioner.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r2.speaker: ابن جرير
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r2.claim: Ibn Jarīr interprets مغفرة as concealing the needy person’s poverty and poor condition.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r3.claim: Another reported reading addresses the petitioner, urging restrained, courteous requests and forbidding a display of wealth when not needed; either a kind reply or concealment can benefit more durably than harmful charity.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r4.claim: The comparison shares only the general quality of benefit: the benefit of kind speech and forgiveness endures, while the benefit of charity paired with harm disappears; خير may also mean better than nothing.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r5.claim: A cited poet says a gracious refusal is dearer than giving; another says that even without money, a gentle character can offer either generosity or a kind response.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660#2/r6.claim: قول is an indefinite subject licensed by its description; مغفرة coordinates as a second subject, with an omitted description such as forgiveness from the giver, petitioner, or God.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p660/r5.claim: A kind reply from the person asked, and forgiveness when a petitioner presses or speaks offensively, are better than charity followed by harm; forgiveness may also be God’s forgiveness or the petitioner’s excuse for refusal.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r1.speaker: المهدوي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r1.claim: Al-Mahdawī and others parse two clauses, with an omitted predicate after قول: “a kind word is preferable, and forgiveness is better”; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says this loses rhetorical smoothness, and Abū Ḥayyān agrees.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r2.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r2.claim: قول معروف could instead be the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning “what is commanded is a kind word”; المن need not be repeated in يتبعها because harm includes it.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r3.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v2p661/r3.claim: God is غني because He needs no charity and حليم because He delays punishment; another reading stresses that He needs no giver who reproaches or harms and forbears from hastening punishment, carrying warning.

SAMIN-DURR:2:263#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:263#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:263#2/r1.claim: يتبعها أذى is a genitive adjective qualifying صدقة.

SAMIN-DURR:2:263#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:263#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:263#2/r2.claim: The phrase does not repeat منّ because harm includes reproach and other forms; the earlier verse names reproach explicitly because donors often commit it and find it hard to avoid.

SAMIN-DURR:2:263#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:263#2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:263#2/r3.claim: Reproach precedes harm in the wording because it is especially common among donors.

SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r1.claim: One parse makes قول معروف a subject licensed by description or coordination, مغفرة its coordinate, and خير the predicate of both; مغفرة may be qualified as from the asker or God.

SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r2.claim: On that parse, an omitted noun may be supplied as سبب مغفرة, since divine forgiveness cannot be compared in merit with a human act.

SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r3.claim: Alternatively, مغفرة can mean the donor’s overlooking and patience with the poor recipient, requiring no omitted noun.

SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r4.speaker: المهدوي
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r4.claim: Another parse gives قول معروف an omitted predicate such as أمثل or أولى بكم, while مغفرة is a separate subject with خير as predicate.

SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r5.speaker: ابن عطية
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the two-sentence analysis loses the meaning’s elegance.

SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:2:263/r6.claim: A third parse makes the phrase a predicate of an omitted subject: what is commanded is a kind word.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r3.claim: A kind word and prayer for a Muslim, together with forgiving verbal or physical wrong, are better than charity followed by harm.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r4.speaker: رسول الله
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r4.claim: A report reaching ʿAmr ibn Dīnār says no charity is more beloved to God than a good word, citing this verse.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r5.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r5.claim: God has no need of His creatures; He is forbearing, forgiving, and overlooking.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r6.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r6.speaker: أبو ذر
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r6.claim: The Prophet warned of painful punishment for three people: one who flaunts what he gave, one who lets his garment trail, and a merchant who uses false oaths.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r7.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r7.speaker: أبو الدرداء
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p693/r7.claim: A report says that a person disobedient to parents, one who flaunts charity, a habitual wine drinker, and a denier of divine decree do not enter Paradise; other transmitters report a similar version.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p694/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p694/r1.speaker: ابن عمر
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p694/r1.claim: Another prophetic report lists the disobedient child, habitual wine drinker, and person who flaunts gifts among three whom God will not look upon at the Resurrection.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p694/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p694/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v1p694/r2.claim: A report through Mujāhid says habitual wine drinkers, those disobedient to parents, and those who flaunt gifts do not enter Paradise; other transmissions attribute related reports to Mujāhid from Abū Saʿīd and Abū Hurayra.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r6.claim: A kind, appropriate word does not wound the questioner's heart, taking account of both the questioner's and speaker's circumstances.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r7.claim: If a petitioner becomes angry at a courteous refusal, forgiving him and speaking kindly is better than giving charity that is followed by hurt.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r8.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r8.claim: Charity manifests trust in unseen provision and its divine replacement, but the harm that follows may outweigh the benefit; God is self-sufficient and accepts only what He permits.

BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r9.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r9.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p516/r9.claim: God is forbearing: He does not immediately punish disobedience but continues to provide for and support the sinner despite disobedience and ingratitude.

DURR-FULL:v2p43/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r1.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r1.claim: A report reaching Amr says no charity is dearer to God than a kind word, invoking this verse.

DURR-FULL:v2p43/r2.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r2.claim: The Prophet calls teaching a Muslim brother knowledge the best charity.

DURR-FULL:v2p43/r3.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r3.speaker: عبد الله بن عمرو
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r3.claim: The best gift a Muslim can give his brother is a wise word that guides him or turns him from error.

DURR-FULL:v2p43/r4.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r4.speaker: سمرة بن جندب
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r4.claim: The Prophet says no charity people give matches knowledge that is spread.

DURR-FULL:v2p43/r5.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r5.claim: A true word heard and taught to a Muslim brother is an excellent gift.

DURR-FULL:v2p43/r6.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r6.speaker: الضحاك
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r6.claim: A good word is a gracious reply such as praying for mercy or provision, without scolding or harsh speech.

DURR-FULL:v2p43/r7.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v2p43/r7.claim: The rich person is complete in wealth, and the forbearing person complete in forbearance.

BURSEVI:v1p344/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p344/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p344/r1.claim: A gracious response means turning away a petitioner kindly; forgiveness covers overlooking persistent or burdensome requests.

BURSEVI:v1p344/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p344/r2.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p344/r2.claim: A kind refusal and pardon are better than a gift followed by harm, because one who both helps and injures the poor loses the reward.

BURSEVI:v1p344/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p344/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p344/r3.claim: The apparent puzzle—how a harmful charity can still be called good—is answered by reading the comparison from the hearers' limited perspective, as in the cited verse about trade and amusement.

BURSEVI:v1p344/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p344/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p344/r4.claim: God needs no charity and can provide the poor by another route; His forbearance delays punishment for boastful givers but does not excuse them.

BURSEVI:v1p344/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p344/r5.speaker: الهدائي
BURSEVI:v1p344/r5.claim: A gracious refusal lifts the petitioner's heart and spirit, while charity first benefits the body; spiritual relief outweighs bodily benefit spoiled by hurtful words.

BURSEVI:v1p344/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p344/r6.speaker: الشعبي
BURSEVI:v1p344/r6.claim: Al-Shaʿbī says a donor who does not consider himself more needy for charity's reward than the poor person is for the gift has invalidated his charity.

BURSEVI:v1p344/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v1p344/r7.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v1p344/r7.claim: Early Muslims guarded against ostentation because it is common and ruinous; in the grave ostentation becomes a snake and miserliness a scorpion, and indulging one vice feeds it.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r1.claim: A kind response to a petitioner—such as wishing God’s mercy or provision, or promising to give later—and overlooking an intrusive request are better than a gift followed by injury.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r2.claim: Another possible reading makes forgiveness God’s forgiveness of the person enduring a difficult petitioner, or the petitioner’s forgiveness of a refusal; the author rejects these as mismatched comparisons.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r3.claim: The proposed alternatives fail because the comparison should contrast two qualities of the same person, and they imply some good in a wholly invalid harmful gift.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r4.claim: The sentence confirms the instruction to avoid reproach and harm; it omits reproach because injury includes reproach and more, and the indefinite opening is licensed by qualification or coordination.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r5.claim: God is independent of people’s charity and commands it for their benefit; alternatively, He rejects charity mixed with reproach, or can provide the poor elsewhere so they need not endure it.

ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v3p34#2/r6.claim: God is forbearing: He delays punishment for reproach and injury, though their perpetrators deserve it; the ending therefore carries both promise and warning.

ELMALILI:2:261-264#2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264#2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264#2/r7.claim: A kind word that gently refuses, together with overlooking faults and answering impropriety with forgiveness, is better than charity followed by hurt.

ELMALILI:2:261-264#2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264#2/r8.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264#2/r8.claim: God is self-sufficient and does not make the poor bear another person's burden of gratitude; He may provide unexpectedly until the poor can give to their former benefactor.

ELMALILI:2:261-264#2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:2:261-264#2/r9.speaker: author
ELMALILI:2:261-264#2/r9.claim: God is forbearing and delays punishment so sinners, including those who hurt recipients, may repent; the delay does not mean they deserve no punishment.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r1.claim: The discussion moves from spending in God's path to charity for needy individuals, where reminders and injury are more likely because donor and recipient know one another personally.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r2.claim: Mann toward a recipient is reminding them of the favor, as already explained.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r3.speaker: الزمخشري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī's wordplay contrasts the sweetness of blessings with the bitterness of reminding: الآلاء first means blessings, then a bitter plant; المن first means manna from heaven and then reminding of a favor.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r4.claim: Adhā is injury or slight harm; here it means explicit condescension, reproaching poverty, or humiliating the recipient, distinct from the reminder itself.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r5.speaker: أبو حامد الغزالي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p43#2/r5.claim: Al-Ghazālī locates the root of reminders in the heart and their outward forms in speech and action; resentment at giving and feeling superior to the poor both arise from ignorance of charity's greater reward and of true human worth.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r1.claim: The sentence is an explanatory resumption; the indefinite قول معروف minimizes the standard, so even a little kind speech is better than charity followed by harm.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r2.claim: Known good speech is what people recognize as acceptable, namely gracious speech, the opposite of injury.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r3.claim: Forgiveness may mean the donor overlooking an insistent or rude beggar, or God overlooking sins because charity was accompanied by kind speech; injury may thus erase charity's reward.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r4.claim: God's richness and forbearance urge believers to rise above stinginess and to pardon the roughness of some recipients.

IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v3p47/r5.claim: Invalidity means failure of a deed's intended legal effect: an obligatory act is not discharged if a pillar or condition fails, while a voluntary act loses reward when a legal impediment prevents it, as here.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r1.claim: The connected themes suggest this passage was revealed as one unit: spending grows seven hundredfold or more, sincere giving bears fruit, ostentation and reminders or harm ruin reward, good wealth should be given, the poor detained in God's path are recipients, and the reward is great.

TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:261-274/r2.claim: The passage orders its teaching around purpose (giving for God, not people), manner (without reproach or injury), quality (good rather than bad wealth), recipient (the needy constrained in God's path), and reward.

TABATABAI:2:264#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:264#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:264#2/r1.claim: A recognized good word is speech customarily accepted by people, with its content varying by circumstance; maghfira originally means covering.

TABATABAI:2:264#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:264#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:264#2/r2.claim: Ghinā is the opposite of need and poverty, and hilm is restraint in the face of unpleasant words or acts.

TABATABAI:2:264#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:264#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:264#2/r3.claim: The better alternative means a kind prayer or gracious dismissal when the petitioner is not offensive, and concealment and pardon if the request is phrased offensively.

TABATABAI:2:264#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:2:264#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:2:264#2/r4.claim: A hurtful donor treats the gift as large and is pained by the request; believers should remove both traits by emulating God's self-sufficiency and forbearance.

ASAD-NOTES:2:262#n259/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:2:262#n259/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:2:262#n259/r1.claim: Asad renders maghfarah in this context as concealing another person's need, following al-Baghawi's explanation.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:262/r3.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:262/r3.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:2:262/r3.claim: If giving would hurt the recipient, kind words, patience, and discretion about their need are ethically and spiritually preferable to giving.

STUDYQURAN:2:262/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:262/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:2:262/r1.claim: Pride in generosity or reminding recipients of their need destroys charitable giving’s merit; a decent word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by harm.

STUDYQURAN:2:262/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:262/r2.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:2:262/r2.claim: R says one should speak kindly to poor people and forgive harm they may cause through rough manner or embarrassment.

STUDYQURAN:2:262/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:2:262/r3.speaker: R
STUDYQURAN:2:262/r3.claim: R says to forgive the poor if their requests cause trouble or discomfort.
